summary: Captures the problem statement for the Softwires Working Group, which developed standards for connecting IPv4 networks across IPv6-only networks and the reverse. It describes discovery, control, and encapsulation needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A softwire is a managed tunnel that carries one IP address family through a network that supports another. This RFC describes the hub-and-spoke and mesh problems that softwire standards were intended to address.

questions: how to connect ipv4 networks over ipv6
how can ipv6 cross an ipv4 network
subtitle: The two network situations that require tunnels between IPv4 and IPv6

tldr.problem: IPv4-only and IPv6-only networks cannot route each other's packets directly. A network may need to carry one address family across infrastructure that supports only the other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two problem settings for softwires: customer hub-and-spoke access and mesh connectivity between address-family border routers.
tldr.outcome: This Informational problem statement defines scope and requirements for the Softwires Working Group; it does not specify a tunneling protocol.

today: RFC 4925 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the problem scope for softwire standards and does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: Why Softwires Are Needed
sections.content:
During the transition between IPv4 and IPv6, networks may support only one address family along part of a route. Local networks may contain IPv4-only and IPv6-only applications, while a transit network may not carry both kinds of packets natively.

The RFC uses “softwire” for a tunnel created and managed through a control protocol between endpoints. The working group was tasked with standards for discovery, control and encapsulation, with an emphasis on reusing or extending existing technology. Only traffic that cannot otherwise cross the address-family mismatch should use the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks can carry IPv4 packets but not IPv6 packets, or the reverse. A softwire tunnels the traffic that cannot cross the network directly.

sections.title: Softwire Endpoints and Address Families
sections.content:
The softwire transport header address family (STH AF) is the outer IP family used to cross the tunnel network. The softwire payload header address family (SPH AF) is the IP family carried inside. For example, an IPv6 packet carried through an IPv4 network uses IPv4 as its transport family and IPv6 as its payload family.

The softwire initiator starts the tunnel, usually in a customer network. The softwire concentrator terminates it in a service-provider network. In the mesh case, address-family border routers (AFBRs) sit at the edges of a backbone that carries one family and can encapsulate packets of the other.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel has an outer address family for crossing the network and an inner family for the packet being carried. Its two endpoints start and terminate that tunnel.

sections.title: Hub-and-Spoke Access Networks
sections.content:
In the hub-and-spoke problem, many customer networks connect to a smaller number of carrier softwire concentrators. The customer-side initiator may be a dual-stack host, a customer router, or a device behind a router that cannot be upgraded. The RFC describes the reverse address-family cases as well.

The tunnel must work when the customer's address is assigned dynamically and may need to cross NAT or port-address translation. The customer should not need to send traffic through the tunnel when the native network can already carry it. A carrier must be able to scale the model by adding concentrators, and the softwire must support multicast and appropriate authentication and accounting.
sections.plainLanguage: Many customer networks can connect to a small number of carrier hubs. The tunnel may need to start inside a home or office, even when its existing router cannot run both address families.

sections.title: Mesh Connectivity Across a Single-Family Core
sections.content:
In the mesh problem, a backbone supports one address family while carrying packets of another between customer networks. Dual-stack AFBRs at the network edge exchange routing information for the carried family and tunnel packets across the core. The design aims to avoid changes to the core routers.

The RFC does not require one encapsulation for mesh softwires. It lists L2TPv3, IP-in-IP, MPLS, GRE and IPsec as options that a solution should accommodate, selected according to policy. Softwires should be available without adding appreciable delay to packets, and a solution must address multicast and security for both control information and traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: In a mesh, border routers tunnel packets directly across a backbone that cannot carry those packets natively. The core can remain unchanged while its border routers handle both address families.

sections.title: Shared Requirements and Security
sections.content:
Both models need automatic setup, failure detection and management tools such as logging and accounting. Hub-and-spoke solutions must support customer authentication and authorization; mesh solutions need ways to authenticate participating peers and protect control data from modification or impersonation.

The RFC says that the control and data planes must be able to provide privacy, integrity and replay protection where needed, with IPsec support required in the mesh case. Tunneling may bypass site ingress filters that inspect only the outer transport-family header, so operators must consider that effect in their security policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Both tunnel designs need to start, detect failures and support network operations. Their security must match the setting, and filters that inspect only the outer packet may not see the carried packet's addresses.

left.title: Hub and spoke
left.desc: Many customer-side tunnels terminate at a smaller number of carrier hubs.

right.title: Mesh
right.desc: Edge routers tunnel across a backbone that supports only one address family.
